implementation_notes: Installed distributions declare components as entry points, so the configurator reads the configured group from importlib.metadata.entry_points(group=...), resolves each EntryPoint with load() (which imports the module and returns the attribute) and stores the result in a dict repository - the mechanism behind pluggy/pip-style plugin discovery, with no knowledge of file layout required. The select API (group=/name= keyword filtering) needs Python 3.10+; unlink is impossible in-process because modules live in sys.modules and already-handed-out objects stay alive, so replacement means a fresh process (importlib.reload is a development aid, not an unlink).
code_sketch:
from importlib.metadata import entry_points

def link(cfg: dict) -> dict[str, Component]:
    repo: dict[str, Component] = {}
    for ep in entry_points(group=cfg["group"]):        # installed metadata
        factory = ep.load()                            # imports module + attribute
        repo[ep.name] = factory(**cfg["params"].get(ep.name, {}))
    return repo
pitfalls: entry_points() reads the metadata of installed distributions, so components must really be installed in the active environment (editable or wheel); a missing distribution is simply absent from the repository unless the configurator asserts every configured name is present.
The keyword select API requires Python 3.10+; older code must filter the returned EntryPoints by hand, and the pre-3.10 dict-by-group return type was removed in 3.12.

Loading an entry point imports the component module for the life of the process: its import side effects and any state it registers survive 'unlink', and deleting sys.modules entries leaves stale class objects behind.

variants.name: plugin directory scanned and loaded by path
variants.implementation_notes: When components are loose .py files rather than installed distributions, the configurator scans a configured directory and builds each component from a file location: spec_from_file_location(name, path), module_from_spec, then spec.loader.exec_module(module), and finally the configured attribute becomes the component. This is the directory-plugin form used by applications that ship their extensions as plain files; it works anywhere on the filesystem but leaves packaging, dependency resolution and isolation in your hands (importlib.invalidate_caches() is needed when files appear after interpreter start).
pitfalls: exec_module runs the component's code at link time, so the directory must be trusted and non-writable; validate paths, and treat a configuration that points outside it as an error rather than a convenience.
A module loaded by path gets a synthetic name, so relative imports inside it fail unless the containing directory/package is on sys.path or the spec is created with the right package context.

Files created after interpreter start are invisible until importlib.invalidate_caches() is called; a plugin dropped into the directory while the process runs needs an explicit cache invalidation and still cannot be unloaded afterwards.
